title_en: Du Haisheng, Du Mansheng v. Du Xisheng — dispute over property right confirmation

full_text_en:
Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng v. Du Xisheng — Dispute over Confirmation of Property Right

Plaintiff: Du Haisheng, male, 30 years old, a farmer from Pingding County, Shanxi Province.

Plaintiff: Du Mansheng, male, 27 years old, a farmer from Pingding County, Shanxi Province.

Defendant: Du Xisheng, male, 35 years old, a farmer from Pingding County, Shanxi Province.

Third Party: Du Yongsheng, male, 45 years old, a farmer from Pingding County, Shanxi Province.

Third Party: Haiyu, female, 21 years old, a farmer from Pingding County, Shanxi Province.

The plaintiffs, Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng, filed a lawsuit with the Pingding County People's Court of Shanxi Province against the defendant, Du Xisheng, over a dispute concerning the confirmation of property rights to a house. The plaintiffs, Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng, alleged: The three rooms of a bungalow and one stable in dispute were purchased by the third party, Du Yongsheng, for the entire family, as evidenced by the homestead land use certificate. The defendant, Du Xisheng, was now preparing to take this house as his own. The plaintiffs requested that the court confirm that the property rights to the disputed house belonged to the entire family as co-owners.

The defendant, Du Xisheng, argued: The disputed house was purchased by the third party, Du Yongsheng, who intended to transfer it to me at the original price. Therefore, the homestead land use certificate recorded me as the household head. Since the plaintiffs want to contest this property, I can give it up, but it must be returned to the original owner, Du Yongsheng.

The third party, Du Yongsheng, stated: The defendant's contention is true. Because Du Xisheng has a physical disability, I purchased this house with the intention of transferring it to him alone at the original price, excluding other family members.

The Pingding County People's Court found through public trial: The parties to this case are siblings. After their father died in 1977, the third party, Du Yongsheng, got married and lived separately, leaving only their mother, Yang Sanni, the defendant, Du Xisheng, the plaintiffs, Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng, and the third party, Du Haiyu, living together. In 1984, Du Yongsheng purchased three rooms of a bungalow and one stable in the village for RMB 700. In 1986, Du Yongsheng applied for and obtained a "homestead land use certificate" for this property, on which the household head was recorded as Du Xisheng and the family members as five persons. The village's homestead clearance registration form recorded that the five persons listed on the homestead land use certificate were the household head, Du Xisheng, and family members Yang Sanni, Du Haisheng, Du Mansheng, and Du Haiyu. These five persons had managed and used this property for a period of time. In 1987, Yang Sanni passed away. In April 1992, a family dispute arose between the plaintiffs and the defendant. At that time, Du Yongsheng claimed that the disputed property was transferred only to Du Xisheng alone and altered the "five persons" recorded on the homestead land use certificate in his possession to "one person." In July of the same year, Du Xisheng rented the disputed property to a neighbor, Lu Weizhu, for RMB 1,800. Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng filed this action for confirmation of property rights, claiming that the property was jointly owned by the entire family.

The Pingding County People's Court held: The third party, Du Yongsheng, purchased the disputed property for RMB 700. Pursuant to Articles 71 and 72 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China, he is the legitimate owner of the property and enjoys the rights to possess, use, benefit from, and dispose of it in accordance with the law. In the homestead land use certificate that he applied for, Du Yongsheng declared that the household head was Du Xisheng and the family members were the five persons: Du Xisheng, Yang Sanni, Du Haisheng, Du Mansheng, and Du Haiyu. This act constituted an exercise of his right to dispose of his own property, with a genuine expression of intent amounting to a voluntary transfer. The homestead land use certificate is a legally valid document and should be protected. After Du Yongsheng obtained the homestead land use certificate, the five family members headed by Du Xisheng managed and used the property. At that point, Du Yongsheng's ownership of the disputed property had been lawfully transferred to the five persons headed by Du Xisheng as co-owners. After the family dispute arose, Du Yongsheng repudiated the voluntary transfer of property rights and unilaterally altered the entries on the homestead land use certificate, claiming that the property was transferred only to Du Xisheng alone. Under Article 85 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), which provides that "after a lawful transfer of property ownership, if a party repudiates it, such repudiation shall not be supported," Du Yongsheng's repudiation was not supported. Accordingly, on July 18, 1994, the Pingding County People's Court rendered its judgment: The three rooms of the bungalow and one stable in dispute are jointly owned by the five persons: Du Xisheng, Du Mansheng, Du Haisheng, Du Haiyu, and their mother, Yang Sanni.

After the judgment of first instance, the defendant, Du Xisheng, and the third party, Du Yongsheng, appealed to the Yangquan Intermediate People's Court of Shanxi Province, contending that the transfer of the house between Du Xisheng and Du Yongsheng was intended to be at the original price, that the property certificate remained in Du Yongsheng's possession, and that the first instance finding that ownership had been lawfully transferred was inconsistent with the facts.

During the second instance trial, the Yangquan Intermediate People's Court found: The appellant, Du Yongsheng, only orally agreed in 1986 to sell the disputed property to the appellant, Du Xisheng, at the original purchase price, but neither the property nor the purchase price had been delivered between the parties, nor had a written contract or tax payment for the property sale been carried out, and the property ownership certificate remained in Du Yongsheng's possession. The first instance finding that the five persons had managed and used the property for a period of time referred to the fact that the five persons had lived in the house for a period without the property ownership certificate. The first instance finding that Du Xisheng rented the house to a neighbor for RMB 1,800 was inaccurate: in fact, Du Xisheng arranged the rental, but the rent paid by the lessee was collected by Du Yongsheng, and the final agreed rental amount was RMB 900.

The Yangquan Intermediate People's Court held: A homestead land use certificate, issued pursuant to Article 38 of the Land Administration Law of the People's Republic of China, is a document confirming the lawful status of rural residents' use of land for building houses. Only persons holding such a certificate may build houses within the lawfully used homestead area; therefore, the holder of the homestead land use right should be consistent with the owner of the house. The house property ownership certificate is the lawful evidence for confirming house ownership, and other documents cannot replace the effect of the house property ownership certificate in confirming ownership. The appellees, Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng, sought to confirm the ownership of the house based on the entries in the homestead land use certificate; this was improper.

The transfer of house ownership may be either gratuitous (i.e., a gift) or for value (i.e., a sale). Pursuant to Article 128 of the Supreme People's Court's Opinions on Several Issues concerning the Implementation of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People's Republic of China (for Trial Implementation): "...For a gift of a house, if the transfer procedures have been completed in accordance with a written gift contract, the gift relationship shall be deemed established; if the transfer procedures have not been completed, but the donor, according to a written gift contract, has delivered the property ownership certificate to the donee, and the donee has taken possession and used the house according to the gift contract, the gift may be deemed valid, but the donee shall be ordered to complete the transfer procedures later." Since the first instance judgment found that Du Yongsheng had transferred the house ownership without determining whether the transferee had paid consideration, it should have applied the provisions on gifts of houses to this case. However, the house property ownership certificate was still in the hands of the appellant, Du Yongsheng. The appellant, Du Xisheng, and the appellees, Du Haisheng and Du Mansheng, although they had lived in the house, did not take possession and use the house under a gift contract. The first instance judgment's reliance on the entries in the homestead land use certificate and the fact that Du Xisheng and others had lived in the house to find that Du Yongsheng had lawfully transferred the house ownership was contrary to law. Although Du Yongsheng had orally stated that he would transfer the house to Du Xisheng at the original price, he never handed over the property ownership certificate, never received any payment from Du Xisheng, and never actually delivered the property to Du Xisheng for use; instead, he collected RMB 900 in rent from the neighbor, Lu Weizhu. These facts show that the ownership of the disputed house had neither been transferred gratuitously nor for value, but had always remained under the control of the owner, Du Yongsheng. Accordingly, applying Article 72 of the General Principles of the Civil Law and Article 153(1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Yangquan Intermediate People's Court rendered its judgment on November 9, 1994:

1. The civil judgment (1994) Ping Min Chu Zi No. 23 of the Pingding County People's Court is set aside.

2. The three rooms of the bungalow and one stable in dispute are owned by Du Yongsheng.
